Enhancement","color":"fef2c0","default":false,"description":null},{"id":16917452,"node_id":"MDU6TGFiZWwxNjkxNzQ1Mg==","url":"https://api.github.com/repos/numpy/numpy/labels/component:%20numpy.f2py","name":"component: numpy.f2py","color":"009800","default":false,"description":null}],"state":"open","locked":false,"assignee":null,"assignees":[],"milestone":null,"comments":11,"created_at":"2023-12-04T14:09:26Z","updated_at":"2024-11-14T15:28:27Z","closed_at":null,"author_association":"NONE","active_lock_reason":null,"draft":false,"pull_request":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/numpy/numpy/pulls/25307","html_url":"https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/25307","diff_url":"https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/25307.diff","patch_url":"https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/25307.patch","merged_at":null},"body":"The `crackfortran` tool is developed to be a backend for the f2py utility. However, crackfortran could also be very useful on its own.

The use of crackfortran could be demonstrated by the following example:

```
► crackfortran symbol.f90 -show
Reading fortran codes...
        Reading file 'symbol.f90' (format:free)
Post-processing...
        Block: symbol
Post-processing (stage 2)...
[{'args': ['x', 'y', 'symx', 'opt'],
  'block': 'subroutine',
  'body': [],
  'common': {'pltdat': ['model', 'ploter'], 'symbls': ['nsym', 'symbl']},
  'commonvars': ['model', 'ploter', 'nsym', 'symbl'],
  'entry': {},
  'externals': [],
  'from': 'symbol.f90',
  'implicit': None,
  'interfaced': [],
  'name': 'symbol',
  'sortvars': ['model', 'nsym', 'ploter', 'symbl', 'opt', 'x', 'y', 'symx'],
  'vars': {'model': {'attrspec': [], 'typespec': 'integer'},
           'nsym': {'attrspec': [], 'typespec': 'integer'},
           'opt': {'typespec': 'integer'},
           'ploter': {'attrspec': [], 'typespec': 'integer'},
           'symbl': {'attrspec': [],
                     'dimension': ['20', '2'],
                     'typespec': 'integer'},
           'symx': {'attrspec': [], 'dimension': ['2'], 'typespec': 'integer'},
           'x': {'typespec': 'real'},
           'y': {'typespec': 'real'}}}]
```

The tool presents the subroutine declaration statements as a JSON that can be consumed by other tools for further analysis.

Everyone who is looking for the Fortran parser should first come across crackfortran, before wasting time on many sloppy half-working parsers on the Internet. In this regard, the importance of crackfortran is currently misrepresented by keeping it in the depth of numpy internals. Therefore, this patch adds changes required to expose crackfortran as an entry point, next to f2py3 and reveal it to the world.

> 
> LFortran supports F77.

[OT Warning]
LFortran supports fixed format Fortran which is not the same as F77. For instance, lfortran gives syntax error to
```
      subroutinefoo
      end
```
which is a valid Fortran 77 source code. A true Fortran 77 parser cannot rely on nowadays tokenizers that LFortran uses. Hence my claim.

```

OK, I see. So, this issue is a consequence of having defects in the basic complex arithmetic of Python or numpy objects. Say, take
```python
>>> z = numpy.array([2, 2], dtype=numpy.complex128)
>>> z.imag[0] *= -1
>>> z
array([2.-0.j, 2.+0.j])
>>> I = numpy.array([0], dtype=numpy.complex128)
>>> I.imag[0] = 1
>>> I
array([0.+1.j])
```
then the sign bit gets easily lost even in non-mixed-mode arithmetic:
```python
>>> z * I
array([0.+2.j, 0.+2.j])
```

> > Although, such issue could be fixed at the documentation level.
> Not sure how it's possible.

One possibility is to adjust the Python array API standard to use a different definition for `arcsin`, say, the one that Hull et al paper uses. This definition ensures that `sign(arcsin(z).imag) == sign(z.imag)` on the arcsin branch cut.

Another possibility is to mention in the Python array API standard that on the branch cut, the arcsin expression is not guaranteed to evaluate to the same value with the arcsin return value when expression evaluation is signed-zero ignorant.

> Same issue affects other elementary inverse functions, e.g. arcsinh

Absolutely. The reason is that in the set of functions {arcsinh, arccosh, arcsin, arccos}, one often implements only one of them, say, arcsin, and the rest of the functions can be expressed in terms of arcsin.","reactions":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/numpy/numpy/issues/comments/2067739323/reactions","total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"hooray":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"performed_via_github_app":null}}

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. #### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. #### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. No reason to not guard against this specific segfault in the meantime #### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. No reason to not guard against this specific segfault in the meantime closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. No reason to not guard against this specific segfault in the meantime closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. No reason to not guard against this specific segfault in the meantime closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. No reason to not guard against this specific segfault in the meantime closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. No reason to not guard against this specific segfault in the meantime closes https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. No reason to not guard against this specific segfault in the meantime #### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. No reason to not guard against this specific segfault in the meantime #### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.svd` with too large matrices may segfault if `m*n > int_max` on large-memory machines (on smaller memory machines it may fail with a MemoryError instead). The root cause is an integer overflow in indexing 2D arrays, deep in the LAPACK code.

Thus, detect a possible error condition in the f2py wrapper and error out early.

#### Additional information
<!--Any additional information you think is important.-->

Suggested by @pearu in https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/14001#issuecomment-2015872894

Adding this kind of check to f2py may still make sense IMO. No reason to not guard against this specific segfault in the meantime ```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> n=32767
>>> b=np.random.rand(n)
>>> m_32767=np.diag(b)
>>> m_32767.shape
(32767, 32767)
>>> V_32767=np.linalg.eigh(m_32767)
 ** On entry to DSTEDC parameter number  8 had an illegal value
 ** On entry to DORMTR parameter number 12 had an illegal value
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/pearu/miniconda3/envs/jax-cuda-dev/lib/python3.11/site-packages/numpy/linalg/linalg.py", line 1487, in eigh
    w, vt = gufunc(a, signature=signature, extobj=extobj)
            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/pearu/miniconda3/envs/jax-cuda-dev/lib/python3.11/site-packages/numpy/linalg/linalg.py", line 118, in _raise_linalgerror_eigenvalues_nonconvergence
    raise LinAlgError("Eigenvalues did not converge")
numpy.linalg.LinAlgError: Eigenvalues did not converge
```
where the exception "Eigenvalues did not converge" is very likely wrong and misleading. With n == 32766, the above example works fine.

The underlying problem is that when computing `lwork` for the lapack `syevd` function using expression `1 + 6 * n + 2 * n * n`, it will overflow when `n == 32767`. This problem is not unique to `syevd` but it exists for all lapack functions that work array sizes are quadratic wrt input sizes.

While switching to lapack implementations that uses 64-bit integer inputs, the overflow issue is seemingly resolved but in fact it is just harder to reproduce because the critical `n` size will be `2147483647` where the issue re-merges when the `lwork` expression above will overflow for int64.

I have implemented a solution to the same problem in JAX (https://github.com/google/jax/pull/19288) that will lead to an overflow exception rather than wrong results or crashes. ```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> n=32767
>>> b=np.random.rand(n)
>>> m_32767=np.diag(b)
>>> m_32767.shape
(32767, 32767)
>>> V_32767=np.linalg.eigh(m_32767)
 ** On entry to DSTEDC parameter number  8 had an illegal value
 ** On entry to DORMTR parameter number 12 had an illegal value
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/pearu/miniconda3/envs/jax-cuda-dev/lib/python3.11/site-packages/numpy/linalg/linalg.py", line 1487, in eigh
    w, vt = gufunc(a, signature=signature, extobj=extobj)
            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/pearu/miniconda3/envs/jax-cuda-dev/lib/python3.11/site-packages/numpy/linalg/linalg.py", line 118, in _raise_linalgerror_eigenvalues_nonconvergence
    raise LinAlgError("Eigenvalues did not converge")
numpy.linalg.LinAlgError: Eigenvalues did not converge
```
where the exception "Eigenvalues did not converge" is very likely wrong and misleading. With n == 32766, the above example works fine.

The underlying problem is that when computing `lwork` for the lapack `syevd` function using expression `1 + 6 * n + 2 * n * n`, it will overflow when `n == 32767`. This problem is not unique to `syevd` but it exists for all lapack functions that work array sizes are quadratic wrt input sizes.

While switching to lapack implementations that uses 64-bit integer inputs, the overflow issue is seemingly resolved but in fact it is just harder to reproduce because the critical `n` size will be `2147483647` where the issue re-merges when the `lwork` expression above will overflow for int64.

I have implemented a solution to the same problem in JAX (https://github.com/google/jax/pull/19288) that will lead to an overflow exception rather than wrong results or crashes. I think something similar is appropriate for NumPy as well.

This might be more of a question than a defect itself, and I originally posted it on the scipy repo (scipy/scipy#16412). Over at pymc, we use some of scipy's linalg methods through the aesara package. To parallelize some tasks, we serialize a compiled function to send it to several worker processes. We realized that some of the compiled functions had references to scipy.linalg.lapack methods, which are Fortran objects and these cannot be pickled (or cloudpickled since we are using the latter for serialization).

I'm not sure if this is intended or not, but since the lapack functions are at the top level of the lapack module, it would be great if these could also be safely pickled.

```python
from scipy.linalg import lapack
import cloudpickle


cloudpickle.dumps(lapack.cpotrf)
```

I would agree that pickling fortranobject could work for specific cases.

Recall, the purpose of fortranobject is to hold a pointer value. So, pickling a fortranobject makes as much sense as pickling a C pointer value, that is, it would be sensible within the current process only.

In general, the fortranobject pointer value either references (i) an array data (e.g. Fortran common blocks or Fortran 90 module data) or (ii) a C/Fortran function symbol (e.g. C pointer to cpotrf function in the scipy.linalg._flapack.cpotrf case).

While in the case of array data, pickling a fortranobject instance could be defined as pickling of an numpy ndarray object that views the fortranobject array data. When sending the corresponding pickled object to another process, the process could create a new fortranobject and unpickle the pickled object into it. In the case of common blocks or F90 module data, this does not make sense because of the static nature of common blocks/F90 module data. What would make sense is that when unpickling, the unpickled data would be inserted into the existing fortranobject that references the corresponding common block/F90 module data in the corresponding target process. So, the success of unpickling will depend on the existence of compatible fortranobject in the target process. This would not be a typical workflow of pickling, imho, and if one would need to mirror the common block/F90 module data of another process, I would recommend implementing this explicitly: create ndarray view of data, pickle it, send it to the target process, unpickle it as an ndarray object, and copy the data into the corresponding fortranobject. In certain cases, all this could be captured into pickling/unpickling fortranobjects but only when one carefully addresses all the concerns that exists when pickling/unpickling static data, in general. This is OT for the use case of this issue.

In the case of C/Fortran symbols, pickling/unpicking a fortranobject has similar issues: the C pointer value must valid in the target process that carries out the unpickle task, that is, the target process must have loaded a library that holds the corresponding C/Fortran symbol and there must exists a mapping in between the C pointer values of the current and target processes. This mapping is defined by the imported names. For example, scipy.linalg._flapack.cpotrf references same functionalities of different processes via Python package structure and it makes more sense to pickle a string `"scipy.linalg._flapack.cpotrf"` rather than the corresponding fortranobject instance that just holds a C pointer value to a C/Fortran symbol.

In sum, it is not an unusual that some Python objects are not meant to be pickled, and I think, fortranobject is one of them: fortranobject is a low-level object that holds a raw pointer value that is generally invalid for all processes other than the one that created the fortranobject.

Or to put it another way, it would make more sense to serialize the process how the fortranobject was created so that the target process could reproduce it, rather than serializing the fortranobject itself that holds data that would be typically invalid for target processes.","reactions":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/numpy/numpy/issues/comments/1221583830/reactions","total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"hooray":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"performed_via_github_app":null}}

This draft PR implements the F2PY frontend with `argparse` library. The aim is to split up one big [f2py2e.py](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/f2py/f2py2e.py) into 2 files. One file `f2pyarg.py` is responsible for parsing arguments file while other `service.py` deals with `f2py` core functionalities.

Some upcoming goals are:

- [x] Implement [run_main()](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/0f7eaf8971541e9f7e99c91b3a21e007f9d64c0c/numpy/f2py/f2py2e.py#L411). It is the function responsible for generating wrappers and `.pyf` files.
- [x] Implement [run_compile()](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/0f7eaf8971541e9f7e99c91b3a21e007f9d64c0c/numpy/f2py/f2py2e.py#L505) responsible for compiling and building shared libraries.
- [ ] Decide and implement deprecation of flags. For ex. - `--f2py-wrapper-output`, `--skip-empty-wrappers`
- [ ] Code cleanup. Will involve refactoring and deciding which flags belong to which subparser.

This draft PR implements the F2PY frontend with `argparse` library. The aim is to split up one big [f2py2e.py](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/f2py/f2py2e.py) into 2 files. One file `f2pyarg.py` is responsible for parsing arguments file while other `service.py` deals with `f2py` core functionalities.

Some upcoming goals are:

- [x] Implement [run_main()](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/0f7eaf8971541e9f7e99c91b3a21e007f9d64c0c/numpy/f2py/f2py2e.py#L411). It is the function responsible for generating wrappers and `.pyf` files.
- [x] Implement [run_compile()](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/0f7eaf8971541e9f7e99c91b3a21e007f9d64c0c/numpy/f2py/f2py2e.py#L505) responsible for compiling and building shared libraries.
- [ ] Decide and implement deprecation of flags. For ex. - `--f2py-wrapper-output`, `--skip-empty-wrappers`
- [ ] Code cleanup. Will involve refactoring and deciding which flags belong to which subparser.

This draft PR implements the F2PY frontend with `argparse` library. The aim is to split up one big [f2py2e.py](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/main/numpy/f2py/f2py2e.py) into 2 files. One file `f2pyarg.py` is responsible for parsing arguments file while other `service.py` deals with `f2py` core functionalities.

Some upcoming goals are:

- [x] Implement [run_main()](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/0f7eaf8971541e9f7e99c91b3a21e007f9d64c0c/numpy/f2py/f2py2e.py#L411). It is the function responsible for generating wrappers and `.pyf` files.
- [x] Implement [run_compile()](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/0f7eaf8971541e9f7e99c91b3a21e007f9d64c0c/numpy/f2py/f2py2e.py#L505) responsible for compiling and building shared libraries.
- [ ] Decide and implement deprecation of flags. For ex. - `--f2py-wrapper-output`, `--skip-empty-wrappers`
- [ ] Code cleanup. Will involve refactoring and deciding which flags belong to which subparser.

# Introduction

This page documents how to install different versions of CUDA toolkit to a server and how to use these from conda environments.

# Using CUDA toolkit

In the server, `/usr/local/cuda` refers to the latest installed CUDA toolkit version. However, sometimes one needs to use older versions of CUDA toolkit as well.

Use the following commands for setting up the environment for a particular version of the CUDA toolkit:
```
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-<MAJOR.MINOR.MICRO>
export PATH=$CUDA_HOME/bin:$PATH
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$CUDA_HOME/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
export LDFLAGS="$LDFLAGS -Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_HOME/lib64 -Wl,-rpath-link,$CUDA_HOME/lib64 -L$CUDA_HOME/lib64"
```
For convenience, one can use one of the following commands:
```
. /usr/local/cuda/env.sh
. /usr/local/cuda-11.5.0/env.sh
. /usr/local/cuda-11.4.2/env.sh
. /usr/local/cuda-11.1.0/env.sh
. /usr/local/cuda-11.0.3/env.sh
. /usr/local/cuda-10.2.89/env.sh
. /usr/local/cuda-10.1.243/env.sh
. /usr/local/cuda-10.0.130/env.sh
. /usr/local/cuda-9.2.148/env.sh
```
See [set_cuda_env.sh](https://github.com/Quansight/pearu-sandbox/blob/master/set_cuda_env.sh) for the source code of `env.sh`.

# Installing CUDA driver and toolkits (for sudoers only)

## Getting CUDA installers

To get the latest CUDA toolkit package, use the `wget` command from [cuda-downloads for Ubuntu 18.04](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-downloads?target_os=Linux&target_arch=x86_64&target_distro=Ubuntu&target_version=1804&target_type=runfilelocal)

Earlier versions can be downloaded as follows:

## Installing the driver

Before installing the NVIDIA driver, check if the driver already
exists in the system (try running `nvidia-smi`). Skip this step if it
does (see the Updating the driver section below).

Run the installer of the latest CUDA toolkit and unselect all components except the Driver:
```
sudo sh /usr/local/src/cuda-installers/cuda_10.1.243_418.87.00_linux.run
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ CUDA Installer                                                               │
│ - [X] Driver                                                                 │
│      [X] 418.87.00                                                           │
│ + [ ] CUDA Toolkit 10.1                                                      │
│   [ ] CUDA Samples 10.1                                                      │
│   [ ] CUDA Demo Suite 10.1                                                   │
│   [ ] CUDA Documentation 10.1                                                │
│   Options                                                                    │
│   Install                                                                    │
...
```
and run Install. When successful, try `nvidia-smi` to see if the driver is able to detect the GPU cards correctly.

## Updating the driver

Run the installer of the latest CUDA toolkit and unselect all components except the Driver. For instance:

```
sudo sh /usr/local/src/cuda-installers/cuda_11.5.0_495.29.05_linux.run
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ CUDA Installer                                                               │
│ - [X] Driver                                                                 │
│      [X] 495.29.05                                                           │
│ + [ ] CUDA Toolkit 11.5                                                      │
│   [ ] CUDA Samples 11.5                                                      │
│   [ ] CUDA Demo Suite 11.5                                                   │
│   [ ] CUDA Documentation 11.5                                                │
│   Options                                                                    │
│   Install                                                                    │
...
```
and run Install. When successful, try `nvidia-smi` to see if the driver is able to detect the GPU cards correctly.

If the driver update failed, check out the content of `/var/log/nvidia-installer.log`.

Typically, the driver update fails when the installer is not able to remove old kernel module. Check the output of `sudo lsmod | grep nvidia` and try unloading the drivers manually using `rmmod`. If a module cannot be unloaded, check the output of `sudo lsof | grep nvidia` and `sudo ps aux | grep nvidia` for programs that are using `nvidia` driver or `nvidia-smi`, and close these programs.

Closes #20853.

Some alternatives were suggested in the issue, namely disabling all checks, which is still an option but seems sub-optimal.

However, there are some implementation notes which are important.

This PR changes the behaviour of the **python caller**, which is now responsible for being the right size. That is:

```fortran
subroutine foo(is_, ie_, arr, tout)
 implicit none
 integer :: is_,ie_
 real, intent(in) :: arr(is_:ie_)
 real, intent(out) :: tout(is_:ie_)
 tout = arr
end
```

After compiling `f2py -m blah blah.f90`, this can be called with:

```python
import numpy as np
import blah
xlow = -6
xhigh = 4
xvec = np.arange(12)
def ubound(xl, xh):
  return abs(xl) + abs(xh) + 1
rval = blah.foo(is_ = xlow, ie_ xhigh,
         arr = xvec[:ubound(xlow, xhigh))
expval = np.arange(11, dtype = np.float32)
np.allclose(rval, expval) 
```

Closes #20853.

Some alternatives were suggested in the issue, namely disabling all checks, which is still an option but seems sub-optimal.

However, there are some implementation notes which are important.

This PR changes the behaviour of the **python caller**, which is now responsible for being the right size. That is:

```fortran
subroutine foo(is_, ie_, arr, tout)
 implicit none
 integer :: is_,ie_
 real, intent(in) :: arr(is_:ie_)
 real, intent(out) :: tout(is_:ie_)
 tout = arr
end
```

After compiling `f2py -m blah blah.f90`, this can be called with:

```python
import numpy as np
import blah
xlow = -6
xhigh = 4
xvec = np.arange(12)
def ubound(xl, xh):
  return abs(xl) + abs(xh) + 1
rval = blah.foo(is_ = xlow, ie_ xhigh,
         arr = xvec[:ubound(xlow, xhigh))
expval = np.arange(11, dtype = np.float32)
np.allclose(rval, expval) 
```

Essentially, the caller is now responsible in this scenario for ensuring that the **size** of the array passed in is correct, and this means for the most part that the slice should be calculated as Closes #20853.

Some alternatives were suggested in the issue, namely disabling all checks, which is still an option but seems sub-optimal.

However, there are some implementation notes which are important.

This PR changes the behaviour of the **python caller**, which is now responsible for being the right size. That is:

```fortran
subroutine foo(is_, ie_, arr, tout)
 implicit none
 integer :: is_,ie_
 real, intent(in) :: arr(is_:ie_)
 real, intent(out) :: tout(is_:ie_)
 tout = arr
end
```

After compiling `f2py -m blah blah.f90`, this can be called with:

```python
import numpy as np
import blah
xlow = -6
xhigh = 4
xvec = np.arange(12)
def ubound(xl, xh):
  return abs(xl) + abs(xh) + 1
rval = blah.foo(is_ = xlow, ie_ xhigh,
         arr = xvec[:ubound(xlow, xhigh))
expval = np.arange(11, dtype = np.float32)
np.allclose(rval, expval) 
```

Essentially, the caller is now responsible in this scenario for ensuring that the **size** of the array passed in is correct, and this means for the most part that the slice should be calculated as Closes #20853.

Some alternatives were suggested in the issue, namely disabling all checks, which is still an option but seems sub-optimal.

However, there are some implementation notes which are important.

This PR changes the behaviour of the **python caller**, which is now responsible for being the right size. That is:

```fortran
subroutine foo(is_, ie_, arr, tout)
 implicit none
 integer :: is_,ie_
 real, intent(in) :: arr(is_:ie_)
 real, intent(out) :: tout(is_:ie_)
 tout = arr
end
```

After compiling `f2py -m blah blah.f90`, this can be called with:

```python
import numpy as np
import blah
xlow = -6
xhigh = 4
xvec = np.arange(12)
def ubound(xl, xh):
  return abs(xl) + abs(xh) + 1
rval = blah.foo(is_ = xlow, ie_ xhigh,
         arr = xvec[:ubound(xlow, xhigh))
expval = np.arange(11, dtype = np.float32)
np.allclose(rval, expval) 
```

Closes #20853.

Some alternatives were suggested in the issue, namely disabling all checks, which is still an option but seems sub-optimal.

However, there are some implementation notes which are important.

This PR changes the behaviour of the **python caller**, which is now responsible for being the right size. That is:

```fortran
subroutine foo(is_, ie_, arr, tout)
 implicit none
 integer :: is_,ie_
 real, intent(in) :: arr(is_:ie_)
 real, intent(out) :: tout(is_:ie_)
 tout = arr
end
```

After compiling `f2py -m blah blah.f90`, this can be called with:

```python
import numpy as np
import blah
xlow = -6
xhigh = 4
xvec = np.arange(12)
def ubound(xl, xh):
  return abs(xl) + abs(xh) + 1
rval = blah.foo(is_ = xlow, ie_ xhigh,
         arr = xvec[:ubound(xlow, xhigh))
expval = np.arange(11, dtype = np.float32)
np.allclose(rval, expval) 
```

Closes #20853.

Some alternatives were suggested in the issue, namely disabling all checks, which is still an option but seems sub-optimal.

However, there are some implementation notes which are important.

This PR changes the behaviour of the **python caller**, which is now responsible for being the right size. That is:

```fortran
subroutine foo(is_, ie_, arr, tout)
 implicit none
 integer :: is_,ie_
 real, intent(in) :: arr(is_:ie_)
 real, intent(out) :: tout(is_:ie_)
 tout = arr
end
```

After compiling `f2py -m blah blah.f90`, this can be called with:

```python
import numpy as np
import blah
xlow = -6
xhigh = 4
xvec = np.arange(12)
def ubound(xl, xh):
  return abs(xl) + abs(xh) + 1
rval = blah.foo(is_ = xlow, ie_ xhigh,
         arr = xvec[:ubound(xlow, xhigh))
expval = np.arange(11, dtype = np.float32)
np.allclose(rval, expval) 
```

Consider the following F90 snippet, let's call that `myext.f90`.
```f90
subroutine h2dmpmp_vec(expn1, nterms, expn2, nvcount)
  implicit none
  integer, intent(in) :: nvcount
  complex*16, intent(in) :: expn1(-(nterms):nterms,nvcount)
  integer, intent(in) :: nterms
  complex*16, intent(out) :: expn2(-(nterms):nterms,nvcount)

  expn2 = expn1
end
```
(Excerpted and simplified from code generated by https://github.com/inducer/pyfmmlib/.)

Then run this line and get the following output:
```sh
$ f2py -c myext.f90; python -c "import untitled; print(untitled.h2dmpmp_vec.__doc__)"
# (SNIP gobs of compiler warnings)
expn2 = h2dmpmp_vec(expn1,[nterms,nvcount])

Wrapper for ``h2dmpmp_vec``.

Parameters
----------
expn1 : input rank-2 array('D') with bounds (1 + 2 * nterms,nvcount)

Other Parameters
----------------
nterms : input int, optional
    Default: shape(expn1, 0)
nvcount : input int, optional
    Default: shape(expn1, 1)

Returns
-------
expn2 : rank-2 array('D') with bounds (1 + 2 * nterms,nvcount)
```

Observe the default for `nterms` is given as `shape(expn1, 0)` when it should be `(-1 + shape(expn1, 0)) / 2`. If you remove `nvcount` from the shapes of `expn1` and `expn2`, f2py will produce that.

Maybe this issue is related to #19805?

cc @pearu

```
>>> import sys, numpy; print(numpy.__version__, sys.version)
1.22.0 3.10.1 (main, Dec 16 2021, 23:04:04) [GCC 11.2.0]
```

Describe the issue:

Consider the following F90 snippet, let's call that `myext.f90`.
```f90
subroutine h2dmpmp_vec(expn1, nterms, expn2, nvcount)
  implicit none
  integer, intent(in) :: nvcount
  complex*16, intent(in) :: expn1(-(nterms):nterms,nvcount)
  integer, intent(in) :: nterms
  complex*16, intent(out) :: expn2(-(nterms):nterms,nvcount)

  expn2 = expn1
end
```
(Excerpted and simplified from code generated by https://github.com/inducer/pyfmmlib/.)

Then run this line and get the following output:
```sh
$ f2py -c myext.f90; python -c "import untitled; print(untitled.h2dmpmp_vec.__doc__)"
# (SNIP gobs of compiler warnings)
expn2 = h2dmpmp_vec(expn1,[nterms,nvcount])

Wrapper for ``h2dmpmp_vec``.

Parameters
----------
expn1 : input rank-2 array('D') with bounds (1 + 2 * nterms,nvcount)

Other Parameters
----------------
nterms : input int, optional
    Default: shape(expn1, 0)
nvcount : input int, optional
    Default: shape(expn1, 1)

Returns
-------
expn2 : rank-2 array('D') with bounds (1 + 2 * nterms,nvcount)
```

Observe the default for `nterms` is given as `shape(expn1, 0)` when it should be `(-1 + shape(expn1, 0)) / 2`. If you remove `nvcount` from the shapes of `expn1` and `expn2`, f2py will produce that.

Maybe this issue is related to #19805?

cc @pearu

```

  ewarn(

  ewarn(
Reading fortran codes...
	Reading file 'build/src.linux-x86_64-3.10/scipy/linalg/flapack.pyf' (format:free)
Post-processing...
[...]
```

The warnings appear to be triggered with expressions in `dimension` attributes in a `.pyf` that use a mix of comparisons, logical operators and ternary operators.  E.g.
```
    integer intent(out),dimension((compute_v?(2*(*range=='A'||(*range=='I' && iu-il+1==n)?n:0)):0)),depend(n,iu,il,compute_v,range) :: isuppz

```

Further down the build log, we have similar warnings when building `specfun`:
```
[...]
creating build/src.linux-x86_64-3.10/scipy/special
INFO: f2py options: ['--no-wrap-functions']
INFO: f2py: scipy/special/specfun.pyf
/home/warren/py3.10.1/lib/python3.10/site-packages/numpy/f2py/symbolic.py:1508: ExprWarning: fromstring: treating '(int)v' as symbol (original=(int)v+1)
  ewarn(
/home/warren/py3.10.1/lib/python3.10/site-packages/numpy/f2py/symbolic.py:1508: ExprWarning: fromstring: treating '(int)v' as symbol (original=abs((int)v)+2)
  ewarn(
Reading fortran codes...
	Reading file 'scipy/special/specfun.pyf' (format:free)
Post-processing...
[...]
```
The relevant code in `specfun.pyf` is
```
            double precision intent(out),depend(v),dimension((int)v+1) :: vl
            double precision intent(out),depend(v),dimension((int)v+1) :: dl
```

I don't know if the warnings are harmless, and I don't know if this is something that we should fix in our `.pyf` files, or if this is a f2py bug (ping @pearu).  Whatever the cause, it would be nice to eliminate these warnings.

Normally, a non-void call-back function is expected to return a value, that is, the user-provided Python function ought to return a numeric value. However, if it returns `None` (as specified by a user), then `(capi_j > capi_i)` is `false` and the value of `return_value` is undefined. Since this undefined behavior is under the user's control, f2py allows it, although it will be silent. Initializing `return_value` to `0` (for the sake of silencing the compiler) makes this undefined behavior even more silent.

To fix this issue, we have the following objectives:
1. As a primary one, enforce users to write well-defined code (non-void call-backs should always return a value)
2. Silence the compiler as a secondary objective (initialize `return_value`)
3. The change should be non-BC-breaking (cannot raise an exception when a user callback does not provide a return value, for instance)

I suggest the following solution:
1. When a non-void user callback does not provide a return value, trigger a warning. The corresponding code should be inserted here as `else` block to `if (capi_j > capi_i)`: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/blob/fb0cdc331e0f559e2237fa2e077a4e712f1fee36/numpy/f2py/cb_rules.py#L235
2. Initialize `return_value`. This will be trickier as the return type can be any scalar, including `complex`. The initialization can be carried out in the same `else` block as in 1.
